newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Efforts grow to avert BA strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Efforts grow to avert BA strike.

text.p: Efforts to avert a strike next week at British Airways Plc moved up a gear on Wednesday as union leaders representing BA cabin crew said they were willing to hold talks with the airline.
However it was unclear when negotiations would take place.

As pressure mounted on BA to find a solution to the action, due to start next Wednesday, ten mainly left-wing MPs of the ruling Labour party entered the fray, criticising BA chief executive Robert Ayling for what they called the "worst kind of macho management" in separate disputes with the airline's ground staff and cabin crew.
The members of parliament, led by left-winger Ken Livingstone, expressed concern that Ayling was preparing for a full-scale confrontation with his workforce.

Political analysts, however, said they did not expect Tony Blair's government to intervene publicly in the dispute. The conflict is being seen as a litmus test of industrial relations under the newly-elected Labour government, which has cultivated links with business.
BA offered arbitrated talks on Tuesday to the Transport & General Workers Union (T&G) after the union backed a three-day strike next week by cabin crew.
The two sides have been locked in a lengthy row over BA's planned pay restructuring, which union officials say would cut cabin crew's salaries.
The prospect of a 72-hour strike next week sent BA's shares into a tailspin with the strike likely to play havoc with holidaymakers' plans if flights are cancelled.

With news that Britain had failed to settle disagreements with the European Union over BA's proposed alliance with American Airlines also weighing on sentiment, BA shares dived to 16 1/2 pence in early trading. At 1155 GMT they stood down seven pence at 687 1/2 pence.
"It's hard to find any good news (about BA) at the moment," a London-based trader said.
Chief executive Bob Ayling wrote to T&G's general secretary, Bill Morris, late on Tuesday asking for talks under the supervision of an independent arbitrator.
But neither BA nor the union could say when talks would begin.
"They would start as soon as practicable," BA spokesman David Wilson said, adding that the airline hoped to make a statement later today.
T&G said its willingness to talk to BA did not mean it was calling off the strike.
"I hope now that we can move on and have talks under the auspices of (conciliation service) ACAS and get a settlement," T&G's Morris said.
The union said it was unclear whether BA was willing to talk specifically about the pay row.

"(Ayling's) letter is very unclear as to whether he's talking about the long-term relationship (between BA and the cabin crew) or this immediate issue. We have to resolve that first," T&G spokesman Andrew Murray said.
BA countered by saying it was willing to discuss the pay dispute.
The new pay structure was accepted by a separate union, Cabin Crew 89. But the larger T&G, which represents almost three-quarters of BA's cabin crew, has opposed it.
BA is also in talks to resolve a separate row with its ground staff over the sale of its catering unit.
Both disputes stem from BA's restructuring efforts to cut 1.0 billion pounds ($1.7 billion) from its costs by the year 2000.
